name: Jonathan Hay

summary.text: Jonathan Hay set up and ran the Harvard Institute for International Development's Moscow operations inside the Russian State Property Committee (GKI) during the USAID-funded Russia project directed by Andrei Shleifer. In 1997 USAID alleged he had invested in Russian government bonds in breach of conflict-of-interest rules and HIID dismissed him; he denied wrongdoing. In June 2004 a federal judge found him liable for two counts of fraud and one of conspiracy; the 2005 settlement required him to pay between $500,000 and $2 million depending on his income over ten years and debarred him from USAID work for five years, without an admission of liability.

sources.title: Harvard in Russia: Conflicts of Interest (John Harvard's Journal)

facts.claim: Hay, described by Institutional Investor as having negligible practical experience at the time, set up Harvard's Moscow operations at Chubais's GKI with Shleifer's approval.
facts.quote: Jonathan Hay had negligible practical experience, but soon, with Shleifer's blessing, he was setting up Harvard's Moscow operations at Chubais's GKI in a drafty government building near Red Square.

facts.claim: The 2004 court opinion records that in the summer of 1994 Shleifer invited Hay to invest in Russian oil stocks with him, and held that Hay's disclosure of his investments to Shleifer did not cure the violation because disclosure would have had to be made to someone at Harvard who was not themselves implicated.
facts.quote: to have prevented his violation of the RGEs from forming the basis of a false claim, Hay would, at a minimum, have had to make disclosure to someone at Harvard whose hands were not themselves soiled.

sources.publisher: U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts (via CourtListener)
sources.title: United States v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, Andrei Shleifer and Jonathan Hay, 323 F. Supp. 2d 151 (D. Mass. 2004), No. CIV.A.00-11977-DPW

facts.claim: In 1997 USAID alleged that Hay had invested in Russian government bonds in violation of its conflict-of-interest rules; Hay denied wrongdoing through his lawyer, and HIID dismissed him from the Russia programs.
facts.quote: The agency alleged that Jonathan Hay had invested in Russian government bonds in violation of its conflict-of-interest rules [...] Through their lawyers, both Shleifer and Hay denied wrongdoing. HIID dismissed Hay and Shleifer from their work on the Russia programs.

facts.claim: On June 28, 2004, Judge Woodlock found Hay liable for two counts of fraud and one count of conspiracy, and held that he and Shleifer were making individual investments for individual benefit rather than acting within the scope of their Harvard employment.
facts.quote: He found Hay liable for two counts of fraud and one of conspiracy. [...] the men were not acting within the scope of their employment by Harvard University, but were making individual investments for individual benefit.

facts.claim: Under the 2005 settlement Hay's payment was set between $500,000 and $2 million depending on his income over the following ten years, and he was debarred from USAID work for five years; he did not admit liability.
facts.quote: Hay's portion of the settlement will fall between $500,000 and $2 million, depending on his income in the next 10 years. [...] Shleifer has also been disbarred from USAID work for two years, and Hay for five.

connections.claim: The U.S. Department of Justice sued Hay, Shleifer and Harvard in September 2000; Hay settled in 2005 for between $500,000 and $2 million without admitting liability.
connections.quote: Hay's portion of the settlement will fall between $500,000 and $2 million, depending on his income in the next 10 years.

connections.claim: As part of the 2005 settlement Hay was debarred from USAID work for five years.
connections.quote: Shleifer has also been disbarred from USAID work for two years, and Hay for five.

openQuestions: Hay's formal title at HIID's Moscow office (often given as general director) was not retrieved from a source this session.
The Crimson (2005-08-05) reports a two-year USAID debarment for both men; Harvard Magazine reports five years for Hay.
